chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Saif ibn 'Amirah, from Mansur ibn Hazim, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who asked another man for a garment on credit (bay' al-'inah). The seller said, 'I do not have it, but here are dirhams; take them and buy a garment with them.' So he took them and bought a garment as he wished. Then he brought it back to him, asking if he should buy it from him. He said, 'Is it not that if the garment is lost, it is from the wealth of the one who gave the dirhams?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'He may buy it if he wishes, and he may not buy it if he wishes.' He said, 'There is no objection to it.'

key_terms.أَبُو عَبْدِ اللَّهِ: Abu Abdillah, referring to Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (peace be upon him).
key_terms.بِعِينَةٍ: Sale on credit (Bay' al-'inah), a transaction where an item is sold on credit and immediately bought back for cash.
key_terms.دَرَاهِمُ: Dirhams, silver coins used as currency.
key_terms.لاَ بَأْسَ بِهِ: There is no objection to it / It is permissible.

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on Bay' al-'inah in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) validates the mechanism of *Bay' al-'inah* by emphasizing that the buyer assumes the risk of loss (*ghurm*) for the garment during the interim period, thereby legitimizing the subsequent resale. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic focus on the transfer of ownership and risk rather than merely the form of the contract, distinguishing it from riba. The Imam’s concise confirmation underscores the practical flexibility of trade laws in facilitating liquidity while maintaining contractual integrity.
